passages.title: The lovers speak and exchange praise
passages.summary: The woman asks to meet her lover. She describes vineyard work that her brothers forced upon her.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: The Church’s Bible Dictionary reports the JST: “the Songs of Solomon are not inspired writings.” How does the woman answer those who stare at her skin?

contextNote.title: Scent brings the lover into the poem
contextNote.text: The opening joins a name with the smell of fine oils. The comparison makes attraction felt through the senses. Wine, scent, and touch belong to the poem’s language of desire. Read these images as poetic comparisons, not a list of objects owned by the lovers. Ancient perfume vessels help make that sensory world concrete.

passages.title: Spring brings an invitation
passages.summary: The lover calls the woman outside as spring arrives. She warns against awakening love before it desires.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: Why does the woman place a warning about love beside spring’s invitation?

contextNote.title: Seasonal change becomes an invitation
contextNote.text: The return of flowers and birds accompanies the lover’s call to come outside. Nature gives desire a shared rhythm and setting. The repeated warning about awakening love places timing beside the invitation.

passages.title: A night search and a royal carriage
passages.summary: The woman searches the streets and finds her lover. Another scene shows Solomon’s guarded wedding carriage. His mother gives him a wedding crown.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman’s night search differ from Solomon’s guarded procession?

contextNote.title: Searching gives desire movement
contextNote.text: The night scene turns longing into movement through streets and questions to guards. Finding the beloved changes absence into physical closeness. The later royal procession widens the poem’s scale without explaining every connection between its scenes.

passages.title: Praise through animals, towers, and gardens
passages.summary: The lover praises the woman through many comparisons. She invites him into the garden.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: What does the woman’s garden invitation add to the lover’s praise?

contextNote.title: The garden describes desire through a place
contextNote.text: An enclosed garden joins beauty with protected access. The following lines name fruit, spices, and flowing water. These images describe the beloved through abundance and invitation. They do not give a route to a garden we can locate. Notice how the woman’s response develops the image rather than merely receiving it.

passages.title: A missed visit and a harmful search
passages.summary: The woman opens too late for her lover. Watchmen beat her and take her cloak during her search.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How do the watchmen’s actions change the woman’s search from chapter 3?

contextNote.title: A missed opening changes the scene
contextNote.text: The beloved’s departure turns an expected meeting into searching. The guards now injure the woman instead of merely receiving her questions. Her later praise preserves desire while the encounter remains unresolved.

passages.title: The women offer help
passages.summary: The women offer to seek the lover. He praises the woman above queens and other women.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the women’s offer answer the request she made in chapter 5?

contextNote.title: Belonging follows a question about absence
contextNote.text: Other voices ask where the beloved has gone. The woman answers through garden imagery and mutual belonging. The scene gives her knowledge and speech a central role in restoring the relation.

passages.title: The woman invites her lover outside
passages.summary: The lover praises the woman’s body through comparisons. She invites him to fields, villages, and vineyards.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman take action after hearing the lover’s praise?

contextNote.title: Praise leads into the woman’s invitation
contextNote.text: Descriptions of the body fill much of the chapter. The woman then proposes travel and meeting among growing plants. Her voice gives desire its own direction rather than only receiving another speaker’s praise.

passages.title: Love, family control, and a woman’s answer
passages.summary: The poem compares love with death and fire. Brothers discuss their sister, and a woman answers for herself. Solomon rents out a vineyard.
passages.uncertainty: The map locates named comparisons and groups. It does not trace the lovers’ movements.

lds.text: How does the woman’s answer differ from her brothers’ plans for her?

contextNote.title: The ending places love beyond purchase
contextNote.text: The poem measures love against floodwaters and wealth. The comparisons give desire a force money cannot command. This claim follows scenes of searching, meeting, and separation. Read it as the collection’s final statement about love’s value. A gift of wealth cannot replace the relation the speakers seek.
